etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English formacioun, formation, borrowed from Old French formacion, from Latin fōrmātiō, from fōrmō (“form”, verb); see form as verb. Morphologically form +‎ -ation

definitions.definition: The act of assembling a group or structure. [from 14th c.]

quote.text:
Some cloud formation was confirmed and rainfall was observed over some islands.
.mw-parser-output .k-player .k-attribution{visibility:hidden}Audio (US):(file)

definitions.definition: Something possessing structure or form. [from 17th c.]
The process during which something comes into being and gains its characteristics. [from 18th c.]
(military) A grouping of military units or smaller formations under a command, such as a brigade, division, wing, etc. [from 18th c.]
(geology) A layer of rock of common origin. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 2012, Chinle Miller, In Mesozoic Lands: The Mesozoic Geology of Arches and Canyonlands National Parks, Kindle edition:
quote.text: Over a broad region, the color of a formation may change.

definitions.definition: (military) An arrangement of moving troops, ships, or aircraft, such as a wedge, line abreast, or echelon. Often "in formation".
(sports) An arrangement of players designed to facilitate certain plays.

quote.citation: 2017 May 13, Barney Ronay, “Antonio Conte’s brilliance has turned Chelsea’s pop-up team into champions”, in the Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: N'Golo Kanté embodies both sides of this, a player whose early scratchiness was soothed with glorious results in the new 3-4-3 formation, allowed simply to be his best, most wonderfully mobile, diligent, destructive self.

definitions.definition: The process of influencing or guiding a person to a deeper understanding of a particular vocation.
(category theory) A structure made of two categories, two functors from the first to the second category, and a transformation from one of the functors to the other.
